articles.title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
articles.summary: Researchers at Stanford University genetically altered mice to be able to receive and function with human brain cells.
articles.body:
Neuroscientists in the US have successfully adapted mice to have functioning human cells inside their own brains.

The researchers hope that potential treatments for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diseases that only occur in humans could now be tested on the laboratory rodents.

While mice with brains that are partly human might sound like a Kafkaesque experiment, the scientists said these are not "mice that think like humans".

The animals are genetically engineered - and surgically altered - so that some of their brain tissue is human.

The scientists said their work, published in the journal Nature , was carried out with independent ethical scrutiny.

The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.

Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do.

As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials".

"Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."

The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".

Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."

The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.

While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents , these scientists took that approach to a new level.

First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.

The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue.

These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.

When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.

The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".

After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.

About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.

Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did".

"They don't have any enhancement," he added.

Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."

But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition".

"How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.

'A human program in a mouse environment'

Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".

In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice.

"You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.

These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders.

Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".

This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".

Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer.

In scans of the implanted mice, researchers were able to see connections between the human brain cells and the rest of the mouse brain [S Pasca/Stanford]
The hope is that this will provide a new way to investigate the biology of some human brain disorders [Luis Alvarez]

articles.title: Britain sees second-best butterfly season in 16 years; people counted almost 1.4 million common butterflies and moths; painted ladies jumped by 335%, but scientists are worried
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: The record heat of 2026 made this summer exceptional for butterfly-watching. More than 100,000 volunteers fanned across Britain with notebooks this su.
articles.body: The record heat of 2026 made this summer exceptional for butterfly-watching. More than 100,000 volunteers fanned across Britain with notebooks this summer, tallying nearly 1.4 million common butterflies and day-flying moths. This was the second-best butterfly season of the past 16 years, according to the Big Butterfly Count. Painted ladies surged by 335% compared with 2025. But this butterfly season could be a warning, according to experts.Britain sees a butterfly boom after a summer of record heatThe record heat of summer 2026 has delivered the second-best butterfly season of the past 16 years in Britain. More than 100,000 volunteers counted almost 1.4 million common butterflies and moths this season. Painted ladies, a migratory species that island-hop from sub-Saharan Africa through several generations each summer, did the heavy lifting. There was a 335% rise in their numbers. The Butterfly Conservation organisation recorded their second-highest numbers since the count began in 2010. Other species, such as the holly blue and gatekeeper, also claimed their highest counts ever. The small copper landed third-best in its recorded history. The overall results matched the strength last seen in 2019, a summer that still ranks as the best in the dataset.Butterfly boom may come at a costSo what brought the butterfly boom? Adult butterflies want sunshine and dryness. They got both, in abundance. The five-heatwave season turned out to be perfect for feeding and mating. The significant surge also grabbed human attention. Migratory species like painted ladies rode favourable winds and found conditions ideal for breeding. In pure adult butterfly terms, the weather delivered. But experts believe that the boom may have simultaneously seeded a population crash for next year. Adult butterflies appreciate the bright summer, but for the caterpillars, it's not really promising. The grass, wildflowers and other plants that caterpillars eat withered in the drought.“Adult butterflies love hot, sunny weather for flying, feeding and breeding, and that’s exactly why people saw so many this summer. But a good summer for adult butterflies is not the same as a good summer for butterfly populations,” Richard Fox, head of science at Butterfly Conservation, told The Guardian.“What matters far more is what’s happening on the ground, to the butterflies’ caterpillar offspring and the plants they depend on. The very same weather that made it a good year for butterflies – lots of sunshine and very little rain – could mean we’re actually on course for a population crash, which could take years to recover from.”Population crashes followed the excellent butterfly years of 1976 and 1995, both linked to drought stress. But the trend may not always follow. The droughts in 2018 and 2022 failed to trigger comparable collapses. However, experts still confirm that such hot summers are often bad news for butterflies.But no two droughts are the same. Matthew Oates, an independent naturalist who has kept meticulous butterfly diaries since 1964, pointed to the difference. The 1976 drought was brutal for butterflies, partly because it followed a year of already-dry weather, priming plants to fail catastrophically. This summer was different. Winter 2025 was wet, and early June saw significant rainfall before the drought kicked in. These conditions may have given butterfly foodplants enough water during critical growth stages. He said he was hopeful that last year's wet winter and wet week in early June might prevent the population crash next year.Though it has been a strong summer for migratory butterflies, drought-sensitive species struggled. The speckled wood, green-veined white and ringlet were all recorded in below-average numbers during the Big Butterfly Count, with declines of 44%, 54% and 39%, respectively, since 2011.Fox thinks there are winners and losers in hotter summers: “There will be very few butterfly species that can thrive in the drought situations we had this summer across much of the UK.”Both experts noted that Britain is entering unknown territory in terms of how climate extremes would impact native wildlife and flying insect populations.“If we get another summer of drought or excessive heat that’s really moving into a new future for us and our wildlife, including butterflies,” Fox said.“These last two summers have been way beyond our previous experience. We are out of our comfort zone and we can’t speak with any confidence any more. A lot of our butterflies are behaving more like they behave much farther south in Europe. In some ways it is exciting, but I worry about how relevant our existing, treasured knowledge is. We need every entomologist we can get in this country,” Oates added.

articles.title: Meet Alaina Zhang, the 17-year-old testing whether native seaweed can cut Rhode Island’s coastal nitrogen pollution by 30%
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: At 17, Rhode Island student Alaina Zhang is investigating whether a native seaweed could help tackle one of the state’s coastal pollution problems. Th.
articles.body: At 17, Rhode Island student Alaina Zhang is investigating whether a native seaweed could help tackle one of the state’s coastal pollution problems. Through her project, Harvesting Change, Zhang is studying sugar kelp and its potential to absorb excess nitrogen from coastal waters, where nutrient overload can fuel algal blooms and reduce oxygen available to marine life. Her interest in the issue grew from seeing polluted waterways during her childhood in China and later recognising similar concerns along Rhode Island’s coast. The project has since developed into student-led field research, scientific presentations and environmental advocacy, earning Zhang recognition as a 2025 Gloria Barron Prize winner.How polluted waters in China led Zhang to a Rhode Island research questionZhang’s interest in coastal pollution did not begin in a Rhode Island laboratory. She spent part of her childhood in China, where she saw algae-covered waters and the effects that pollution could have on the communities living beside them. When she later encountered similar concerns along Rhode Island’s coast, the connection stayed with her. Nitrogen enters coastal waters through sources including agricultural runoff and urban sewage. Once concentrations become too high, the resulting algal growth can consume oxygen as it breaks down, leaving less available for fish and other marine organisms.Zhang began looking for a way to address the problem that did not depend solely on removing pollution after it had reached the water. Seaweed offered a different possibility.How native sugar kelp could be used to tackle excess nitrogenSugar kelp is native to the waters around Rhode Island and, like other seaweeds, absorbs nutrients as it grows. Zhang’s Harvesting Change project explores whether that natural process could be put to practical use through kelp farming.According to the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, her research model suggests that growing sugar kelp could remove 30% or more of excess nitrogen under the conditions she examined. The attraction of the approach is partly its simplicity: rather than building an entirely new system to capture nutrients, kelp could use the surrounding seawater as part of the process while producing biomass.That does not make kelp a standalone answer to coastal pollution. Nitrogen still enters waterways from land-based sources, and the amount that seaweed can remove depends on factors such as location, growing conditions and the scale of cultivation. Zhang’s work is instead examining whether kelp can become one component of a wider strategy for improving coastal water quality.How a 17-year-old turned research into a field projectZhang did not begin with an established research programme waiting for her. She contacted researchers herself, including scientists at Brown University and the University of Rhode Island, after reaching out by email. She then worked through the practical side of establishing a field project, including obtaining permits from Rhode Island’s Coastal Resources Management Council and raising money for the work. The result was the first student-run sugar kelp farm in her area.Field research also meant working beyond school and laboratory settings. Marine researchers and field technicians have been involved, while local fishermen have provided experience and knowledge connected to the waters where the project is being carried out. That mix has shaped the project into something larger than a school experiment. Zhang has been testing a scientific idea while also learning how marine research operates in the real world, where permits, equipment, weather, local knowledge and public acceptance all matter.From measurements to a wider coastal questionThe research has developed into two projects examining sugar kelp, nutrient removal and coastal resilience. Zhang is lead author on both, with one manuscript under review by Frontiers in Marine Science, as reported by National Society of High School Scholars (NSHSS). She has also taken the work beyond Rhode Island. At the American Geophysical Union Annual Meeting, she presented her findings as one of its youngest oral presenters.Her kelp biofiltration model has received awards from organisations including the Environmental Protection Agency, NASA, NOAA, the US Air Force and the Rhode Island Clean Water Association. The recognition has given the research a wider audience, but Zhang has continued to spend time explaining the basic problem to people outside scientific settings. She has presented her work at workshops and lectures attended by more than 500 Rhode Islanders. For a project rooted in coastal chemistry and marine biology, communication has become part of the research itself, according to the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes.How Zhang is connecting marine science with environmental policyZhang’s work has also moved into environmental policy. She helped start the Narragansett Bay Resilience Collaborative, which supports policy efforts connected with the health of the bay. She has testified in support of five environmental bills. Among them was the Coastal Habitat Conservation Act of 2023, which was signed into law in 2024.Her involvement has extended beyond state-level policy as well. As a UN Ocean Decade Youth Representative, she has advocated for ocean restoration measures on Capitol Hill. She has also worked with the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management and contributed to an IOC-UNESCO Challenge 10 white paper.There is a practical thread running through those activities. The kelp project asks whether a biological process can help deal with a measurable environmental problem; the policy work looks at the systems and decisions that determine how environmental solutions can be used.How a Rhode Island kelp project became an environmental lessonZhang has spent considerable time bringing environmental science into classrooms and community settings. She serves as a NOAA Ocean Guardian Ambassador and is co-president of her school’s Environmental Science Club. She is also a co-leader of Ecotopia, an NGO supporting youth-led sustainability projects, and has taught elementary school pupils about her experiences in environmental research.That outreach has given her a second audience for the kelp work. A technical finding about nitrogen removal means little to someone who has never encountered the underlying problem. Explaining where the nitrogen comes from, what happens to oxygen in polluted water and how kelp might fit into the picture makes the research easier to connect with everyday coastal concerns. For Zhang, education and research have developed alongside one another rather than as separate activities.“This journey has taught me that leadership doesn’t begin with confidence — it begins with conviction,” she says. “I’ve learned that initiative isn’t about having all the answers — it’s about being willing to try.”

articles.title: A former Australian miner spotted a ripple on Saturn from his backyard in 2024; two years later, he co-authored a world-first discovery of a 10-sided atmospheric wave
articles.summary: Space & Astronomy News: A mysterious ripple spotted on Saturn from an amateur astronomer's backyard in Australia has helped lead to the identification of a giant, 10-sided at.
articles.body: A mysterious ripple spotted on Saturn from an amateur astronomer's backyard in Australia has helped lead to the identification of a giant, 10-sided atmospheric wave around the planet's south pole. Trevor Barry, a former miner from Broken Hill, New South Wales, had been observing Saturn from his homemade backyard observatory when he noticed an unusual feature in 2024. His observations became part of an international research effort that ultimately confirmed the structure using years of observations from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope. The findings were published in the journal Science Advances. According to NASA, the feature is the first large, regular-sided jet pattern identified in Saturn's southern hemisphere.From a backyard telescope to a planetary discoveryBarry has been observing the night sky and collecting planetary images from his observatory in Broken Hill since the early 2000s. His observations of Saturn became particularly important in 2024, when he noticed what appeared to be a subtle ripple developing around the planet's southern polar region. He shared his observations with Agustín Sánchez-Lavega, a researcher at the University of the Basque Country in Spain with whom he had worked since 2008. Barry initially described the feature as a "ripple", but Sánchez-Lavega recognised that it could represent something more significant and encouraged him to continue monitoring it.Barry's observations were not enough by themselves to establish the nature of the feature. However, they provided an important piece of evidence that could be compared with observations from professional astronomical facilities. The research team also included French amateur astronomer Jean-Paul Oger, who, like Barry, contributed observations through the Planetary Virtual Observatory Laboratory, a platform operated by the University of the Basque Country that collects ground-based images of planets from observers around the world.Hubble reveals Saturn's 10-sided waveThe feature eventually emerged as a striking geometric pattern around Saturn's south pole. Rather than forming six sides like Saturn's famous northern feature, the newly identified structure has 10 sides, giving it the description "decagon". NASA says the decagon is a large atmospheric wave embedded within one of Saturn's powerful jet streams. Observations show that it extends through multiple layers of the planet's atmosphere, indicating that it is not simply a feature visible at one cloud level. The discovery was confirmed using observations from Hubble, whose view from space provides sharper images of Saturn without the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere.Researchers examined Hubble observations collected over several years through NASA's Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy, or OPAL, programme. Although the decagon became much clearer in later observations, scientists found evidence that the structure was already beginning to appear in Hubble data from 2023. This long-term record was crucial because it allowed researchers to study the feature as it developed rather than treating it as a single isolated observation.Saturn already has a famous polar shapeThe discovery is particularly intriguing because Saturn's north pole is already home to an extraordinary geometric atmospheric feature. NASA's Voyager spacecraft first observed the six-sided northern polar pattern, known as Saturn's hexagon, during flybys in 1980 and 1981. The structure has remained visible for decades, making it one of the most recognisable atmospheric phenomena in the solar system.Scientists had looked for a comparable structure around Saturn's south pole for years. NASA notes that researchers had been searching for a southern counterpart to the northern hexagon in Hubble observations since 1990. Even NASA's Cassini spacecraft, which studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017, did not reveal evidence of a comparable long-lived formation in the southern hemisphere. Therefore, the newly discovered decagon differs from simply finding another long-established feature. Researchers now have an opportunity to watch a large atmospheric pattern develop.Why the discovery mattersThe southern decagon is not simply a geometric shape appearing in Saturn's clouds. It is associated with the planet's atmospheric circulation and powerful jet streams. NASA researchers say the feature appears to be evolving and strengthening. Its presence in several atmospheric layers could provide clues about how Saturn's atmosphere moves and how large-scale waves form within rapidly rotating giant planets. However, scientists still do not know exactly when the decagon formed or what caused it to develop. The available observations leave an important gap. Saturn's south pole was not readily visible from Earth for part of the period before it came back into view in 2023, while Cassini's mission ended in 2017. That means researchers cannot pinpoint the moment when the structure first appeared.Amateur astronomers played an important roleBarry's involvement highlights how modern planetary science can draw on observations made outside major research institutions. His equipment is based in his own backyard in Broken Hill, yet his observations became part of an international scientific investigation involving researchers, Hubble and data collected over several years. NASA identifies Barry and Oger among the amateur astronomers whose ground-based images helped reveal the subtle southern-polar pattern.For Barry, the discovery also means his hometown appears alongside major scientific institutions and researchers in the work. ABC News reported that he plans to continue observing Saturn from his backyard as scientists try to understand how the feature changes over time.Scientists will keep watching SaturnThe discovery raises several questions that cannot yet be answered. Scientists want to determine how the decagon formed, how long it will survive and whether it could eventually settle into a stable configuration like Saturn's northern hexagon. Further observations from Hubble, NASA's James Webb Space Telescope and computer modelling could help researchers investigate the atmospheric conditions behind the unusual pattern.For now, Saturn has offered astronomers something they had never previously seen there: a large, regular-sided atmospheric wave around its southern pole. And the story of that discovery began not only with a space telescope, but with a former Australian miner watching the ringed planet through a telescope in his backyard.

articles.title: Scientists hung clean moss beside three Russian highways, and the plants began collecting metals linked to traffic pollution
articles.summary: Science News: Researchers in Russia hung bags of moss beside three busy highways to see how much traffic pollution the plants would soak up. Published in the Journa.
articles.body: Researchers in Russia hung bags of moss beside three busy highways to see how much traffic pollution the plants would soak up. Published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials, the study exposed moss collected from a clean background site to roadside air along the Leningradskoye, Yaroslavskoye, and Dmitrovkoye highways in central Russia. After analysing the moss for sixteen elements, the researchers found that traffic-related metals had built up in the plants, with pollution levels varying sharply between the three roads.Why scientists hung moss bags beside three Russian highwaysThe study, titled ‘Impact of traffic-related emissions on air quality assessed via moss bags technique,’ used Sphagnum girgensohnii moss, a species widely recommended for air pollution biomonitoring. Researchers collected clean moss from a background site in Russia's Tver region in May 2023, cleaned it, dried it, and packed it into bags before hanging the bags beside stretches of highway not exposed to any other major pollution sources. The approach let the team isolate the effect of traffic alone on air quality, rather than the mix of industrial and vehicle sources found in most previous moss-bag studies conducted in urban settings.What metals the moss bags collected beside the highwaysAfter exposure, the moss bags were analysed using Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy and a direct mercury analyser to measure sixteen elements, Al (Aluminium), Ba (Barium), Co (Cobalt), Cd (Cadmium), Cr (Chromium), Cu (Copper), Fe (Iron), Mn (Manganese), Ni (Nickel), P (Phosphorus), Pb (Lead), Sr (Strontium), S (Sulphur), V (Vanadium), Zn (Zinc) and Hg (Mercury). Except for phosphorus, the content of every element in the exposed moss matched or exceeded that of the unexposed samples, showing clear uptake of traffic-related pollutants. These elements typically originate from vehicle exhaust, tyre and brake wear, engine corrosion, and dust thrown up from the road surface, all of which the moss absorbed directly from the surrounding air over the exposure period.Why the Leningradskoye highway showed the most pollutionPollution levels differed sharply between the three highways. The most pronounced uptake of elements was recorded at Leningradskoye highway, followed by Yaroslavskoye and then Dmitrovkoye, a ranking researchers linked to differences in traffic density. Aluminium, cobalt, cadmium, manganese, and lead were significantly higher in moss exposed at Leningradskoye than at the other two roads. Statistical analysis also showed that concentrations of aluminium, copper, cobalt, chromium, iron, nickel, and vanadium changed with distance from the road edge, generally falling off the further the moss bags were placed from passing traffic, underscoring how closely tied the contamination was to the highway itself.Moss bags prove an effective tool for tracking Russian highway pollutionThe research was carried out by Inga Zinicovscaia, Omari Chaligava, Nikita Yushin, Dmitrii Grozdov, Konstantin Vergel, and Pavel Nekhoroshkov, based at the Department of Nuclear Physics at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. The team concluded that moss biomonitoring, already widely used across Europe and Asia, proved an effective and inexpensive tool for tracking traffic-related air pollution along stretches of highway free from other contamination sources. Their findings point to vehicle emissions, tyre wear, and brake wear as key contributors to roadside metal pollution, with implications for how such contamination could be monitored more cheaply in the future.

articles.title: In 2013, St Agnes and Gugh began removing invasive rats brought by 18th-century shipwrecks; 12 years later, Manx shearwater breeding sites rose from 22 to a record 225
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: In 2013, a major conservation effort began on St Agnes and Gugh in the Isles of Scilly to remove brown rats that had been harming nesting seabirds. Ac.
articles.body: In 2013, a major conservation effort began on St Agnes and Gugh in the Isles of Scilly to remove brown rats that had been harming nesting seabirds. According to the Isles of Scilly Wildlife Trust, the rats had arrived on the islands following shipwrecks in the 18th century and had become a threat to birds that nested in burrows, including Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels.For this, the Isles of Scilly Seabird Recovery Project was started which brought together local residents, conservationists and wildlife specialists who worked with Wildlife Management International Ltd (WMIL) to look for rat nests and signs of activity before the removal programme began.The intensive baiting operation started in November, 2013. Bait was placed across the islands and monitored every day, with teams checking how much was being taken. By the end of the month, the last evidence of rats had been recorded, but further monitoring continued to make sure the animals had not survived or returned.The recovery of the seabirds has since been tracked through regular surveys. In the latest 2025 monitoring data, St Agnes and Gugh recorded 225 apparently occupied breeding sites (AOBs) for Manx shearwaters, the highest number recorded there. Before the rat removal project, the number of Manx shearwater pairs stood at 22.Rats posed threat Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels are particularly vulnerable to rats because they breed in burrows. Nests can be unsuccessful when rats are present, making invasive predators a major barrier to the recovery of these seabird populations.The islands are home to 13 species of breeding seabirds, with about 17,000 individual birds. The UK holds most of the world's population of both European storm petrels and Manx shearwaters.Before the project, seabird numbers had been declining for years. The removal programme therefore focused on eliminating the brown rats from St Agnes and Gugh rather than simply reducing their numbers. The project says this approach has been used on more than 700 islands worldwide.Seabird breeding increased The first signs of recovery appeared soon after the rats were removed. Conservationists reported that Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels successfully bred on the islands for the first time in living memory. More than 40 chicks of the two species were recorded during the first two years following the removal.The latest monitoring shows that the recovery has continued for Manx shearwaters. There were 22 Manx shearwater pairs before the 2013 project. More than 10 years after rat eradication, there are now almost 200 pairs, while the 2025 monitoring recorded 225 apparently occupied breeding sites.The 2025 survey also found changes in other seabird populations on St Agnes and Gugh. The lesser black-backed gull colony increased slightly to 491 pairs, its highest level since 2014. The kittiwake colony also had 32 apparently occupied nests, which was more than the previous year, although observed breeding success was lower. Signs of cat predation of storm petrels were also recorded.Rat-free islandsSt Agnes and Gugh have remained rat-free since the eradication carried out during the winter of 2013-14. Regular monitoring continues to check for any signs that rats have returned. The islands were officially declared rat-free in early 2017 after further checks. A biosecurity detection dog also visited the islands in February 2025 as part of checks for any returning rats.The islands also faced a possible mouse issue during the winter of 2024. Probable signs were found in chicken feed, prompting four months of monitoring. However, no further signs were found and the team concluded that the mouse had probably died or left before the chicken feed arrived on St Agnes.The success on St Agnes and Gugh has also led conservation groups to consider rat eradication on other islands. A new project is being developed for St Martin's, Tresco, Bryher and about 21 nearby uninhabited islands. Because the islands are closely connected, the proposed operation would need to take place across the whole area at the same time. Since 2025, the team has also held co-design workshops and open days to involve island communities in planning the work.

articles.title: Isro Staff: Not against Pvt Cos; demand due process, transparency; want strategic missions to remain under Isro
articles.summary: Science News: BENGALURU: Private participation has a role in expanding India’s space sector, but publicly funded technology, infrastructure and expertise must be su.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Private participation has a role in expanding India’s space sector, but publicly funded technology, infrastructure and expertise must be subject to transparency, proper valuation and accountability when made available for commercial use, a Joint Action Council (JAC) representing Isro employee associations has said.In a notice circulated among employees, the JAC reads: “We’re not opposed to private participation in the space sector. Indian industry, PSUs and start-ups have an important role in expanding India’s space ecosystem. But private participation must strengthen national capability, not weaken ISRO’s core functions.”It seeks a level playing field, transparency and accountability in the use of capabilities developed through public investment. “Technology developed with public money cannot become a source of private profit without an adequate return to the nation,” the notice says.Public wealthThe JAC has specifically referred to the 410th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, saying it had raised concerns over the transfer of space technologies developed with public funds at prices disproportionately lower than their commercial value. It calls for appropriate valuation, clear pricing norms and licensing fees reflecting the true value of technology.“Public wealth cannot be transferred at throwaway prices or treated as a freebie for private entities,” JAC says. In a section titled “Our Position”, they say: “Isro must retain the complete chain of capability-from research and development to realisation, integration, testing and launch.”.They argue that industrial-scale production of mature launch systems can be expanded through capable public-sector and strategic Indian industrial institutions, provided this doesn’t erode Isro's own technological expertise, manpower, facilities or independent mission capability.The JAC proposes a public-sector-led industrial production system involving NSIL, HAL and other capable strategic Indian aerospace manufacturers for serial production of mature launch vehicles. The stated objective is to increase production capacity while retaining public ownership and accountability and ensuring that Isro retains its technological core.The notice also says Isro must retain the ability to use technologies developed through its work whenever required in the national interest, even when such technologies are made available to private entities.Prioritise NGLV, don’t transfer LVM-3The JAC has called for NGLV to receive the highest priority, with dedicated and permanent manpower for critical areas such as engine development. It has also taken a specific position on LVM-3 technology, saying it should not be transferred in a manner that weakens Isro’s own capability before NGLV is developed and established.“Launch-vehicle technology is not merely a commercial commodity,” the notice says, adding that it has implications for “technological sovereignty, strategic autonomy and national security”. The JAC says strategic technologies, critical infrastructure and national-security launches must remain under effective public control and within the assured capability of the govt and Isro.It also says strategic launches and satellites connected with national security should remain under govt control and be undertaken by Isro.Pvt sector must create capabilityOn start-ups and private enterprises, the notice says they should be encouraged where they create genuine and sustainable national capability.At the same time, it calls for due diligence, proper valuation and accountability when public land, infrastructure and technology are made available for commercial use.The JAC frames the issue more broadly as one concerning scientific capability created through public investment. It says Isro’s launch vehicles, satellites, laboratories, test facilities and launch complexes represent decades of public investment and accumulated knowledge.The notice asks who should benefit from knowledge created with public money and what the nation receives when public technology and infrastructure are opened for commercial use. Its stated principle is that “Public investment must ultimately create public value.”Not competing objectivesIt concludes that the growth of private industry and the preservation of Isro's public capabilities need not be treated as competing objectives. “India needs a strong space industry alongside a strong Isro,” the notice says, while adding that private participation should complement the national space programme rather than come at the cost of the institution that created India's space capability.The JAC says its concerns are not raised out of hostility towards private industry, but over the manner in which public technology, infrastructure and capabilities are transferred or opened for commercial use. It says the scientific capability created with people's money should continue to serve the people.

articles.title: Meet Valerie Warhol and Amy Bianco: The amateur spider hunters who searched a museum drawer and discovered a new species named after John Denver
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: The discovery of a new spider species did not begin in a remote forest or during an expedition. It happened inside a museum, where two amateur spider .
articles.body: The discovery of a new spider species did not begin in a remote forest or during an expedition. It happened inside a museum, where two amateur spider enthusiasts were working through specimens that had remained largely unnoticed for years. Valerie Warhol, an informatics assistant, and Amy Bianco, a part-time volunteer at Carnegie Museum of Natural History, found four rusty-orange trapdoor spiders in a jar while examining the museum’s arachnid collection. Their careful investigation eventually showed that the spiders represented a species unknown to science, which was later named Cyclocosmia johndenveri after the singer named John Denver.Amateur spider hunters’ routine work led to the discovery of John Denver speciesWarhol and Bianco were not setting out to discover a new species. Their regular work involved going through specimens that had not received much attention, identifying them and helping to digitise and catalogue the museum’s holdings. According to Carnegie Magazine, this work is important because turning physical specimens and their labels into detailed digital records allows researchers around the world to access collections that might otherwise remain difficult to study.The scale of that work is enormous. Carnegie Museum of Natural History holds about 18 million invertebrate specimens, making its collection one of the largest in the United States. Yet only around 1% had been digitised when Warhol described the state of the collection. That meant there was still a huge amount waiting to be examined, including specimens that could hold information missed when they were first collected.In spring 2025, Warhol and Bianco were working through the arachnid collection when they came across a jar containing four rusty-orange trapdoor spiders. The specimens had been collected in West Virginia in 1994, but their identity did not immediately fit what was already known about these spiders.The West Virginia specimens did not match any known spidersBianco recognised the spiders as members of Cyclocosmia, a group of trapdoor spiders sometimes known as Oreo cookie spiders because of their large, flattened abdomens marked by ridges. These ridges are thought to help protect the spiders from predators while they remain inside their underground tunnels.The location of the specimens quickly raised questions. At the time, recorded Cyclocosmia species were known from Mexico and the southern United States, while these particular spiders had come from West Virginia. That left two possibilities. One, the specimens could represent a significant extension of the known range of an existing species, or second, they could belong to a species that had never been formally recognised.Warhol and Bianco then examined the spiders more closely. Identifying the species required counting the ridges on the spiders’ flattened abdomens under magnification. The number did not correspond with any known Cyclocosmia species, providing another reason to suspect that the museum drawer contained something unusual.The biologist who helped confirm the unusual spiderThe pair sought help from Danniella Sherwood, a biologist with the Arachnology Research Association in the United Kingdom. Sherwood had recently described a new trapdoor spider from Vietnam and therefore had particular experience with the genus. Her advice directed Warhol and Bianco towards another feature that could help settle the identification.That feature was found on the pedipalps, the small appendages near a spider’s mouth. These structures have several functions, including helping spiders handle food. In mature males, however, they also become reproductive structures used to transfer sperm. Their shape can be highly specific to a species.Using highly magnified photographs supplied by Warhol and Bianco, Sherwood examined the pedipalps of the museum specimens. The photographs showed that their shape differed from those recorded for other trapdoor spiders. This provided the evidence needed to establish that the specimens represented a previously undescribed species.Why the new species carries John Denver’s nameThe spiders’ West Virginia origin led Sherwood to suggest a name connected with John Denver, the singer and songwriter who had a strong association with the state through his song Take Me Home, Country Roads. The resulting scientific name was Cyclocosmia johndenveri.The discovery was formally recognised when its description was published in the scientific journal Natura Somogyiensis. Warhol and Bianco were included as co-authors of the paper, marking an achievement for two people whose work with spiders was not based on conventional academic research careers.Their discovery also illustrates why museum collections can remain scientifically valuable long after specimens are first collected. The discovery emerged not from a fresh expedition, but from patiently revisiting material already held in the institution.What remains unknown about the John Denver spiderEven after the species was officially described, the investigation was not complete. According to Carnegie Magazine, Warhol said that researchers still do not have a female specimen of Cyclocosmia johndenveri. That leaves important aspects of the species’ biology and appearance still to be documented.West Virginia also has relatively little spider research, according to Warhol. The researchers hope that someone might eventually photograph a living example and upload the record. Such an observation could provide another valuable piece of information about the species.

articles.title: Something hit the Moon in 2024 and nobody saw it happen; NASA has now found the 728-foot crater, the biggest recent impact crater known in the Solar System
articles.summary: Space & Astronomy News: The Moon has been taking hits for billions of years, but one of its newest scars managed to escape notice entirely. An asteroid or comet fragment slam.
articles.body: The Moon has been taking hits for billions of years, but one of its newest scars managed to escape notice entirely. An asteroid or comet fragment slammed into the lunar surface in 2024, carving out a crater wider than two football fields without being spotted at the time. It was only months later, buried among millions of images, that scientists realized something extraordinary had happened. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has now helped researchers identify the crater, making it the largest known impact crater formed in the Solar System in recent times.A massive lunar scarAccording to a report by AP News, the crater, named after late lunar scientist Thomas McGetchin, measures about 728 feet (222 meters) across and reaches as much as 141 feet (43 meters) deep. This makes it larger than Rome's Colosseum and roughly three times the size of the previous record-holder discovered by the LRO about a decade ago. The report also states that the scale of the event is particularly striking because impacts this large are thought to occur only about once every 132 years. Scientists therefore see the newly discovered crater as an unusually valuable opportunity to study how the Moon's surface changes after a major collision.The Moon is covered with impact marks from ancient collisions, including some of the largest craters in the Solar System. One enormous lunar basin stretches more than 1,500 miles (2,400 kilometers) across. The newly discovered feature is far smaller, but its recent formation gives researchers something those ancient craters cannot: a chance to study an impact almost as it happened, adds the AP News report.The impact went unnoticedThe collision occurred on the Moon's near side in 2024, but neither Earth-based nor space-based telescopes detected it in real time. The first clue was hiding in the LRO's enormous archive of imagery. Wide-angle photographs taken around the time of the impact were not recognized as significant until August 2025, when researchers identified the newly formed feature.The spacecraft later returned to the area and captured higher-resolution images. Those observations helped scientists confirm the crater's size, shape and connection to a recent impact, with the discovery finalized earlier this year. The collision also disturbed an unexpectedly large area. Material from the impact was thrown across more than 66 miles (100 kilometers) of lunar terrain, giving scientists a detailed look at how debris moves across the surface.The Moon's surface is constantly changingA second study found a roughly 4-mile-wide (7-kilometer-wide) cold region surrounding the crater. Researchers believe the feature is linked to changes in the Moon's upper layer of soil, known as regolith. The findings add to evidence that the lunar surface is being reshaped more quickly than once believed. Data from numerous craters found by the LRO indicate that the Moon's upper inch of soil can be overturned by ejected material about every 80,000 years. hat also means the famous footprints left behind by Apollo astronauts are not permanent. Over geological timescales, fresh impacts and shifting lunar soil will eventually erase them.Preparing for future Moon missionsThe discovery could have practical value beyond understanding lunar geology. As NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon, scientists need to understand how often powerful impacts occur and how far their debris can travel.Researchers are now looking at the potential risk of ejecta from future impacts reaching a lunar base. Understanding those patterns could help engineers design structures capable of withstanding, or reducing the effects of, debris thrown up by collisions. The crater may have appeared suddenly, but its discovery offers scientists a rare glimpse into the Moon's ongoing transformation, and a useful warning for those preparang to live there.Images Courtesy: istock and AP News

articles.title: Three African wild dog brothers left their Zambian pack in 2025; eight months later, they had travelled 4,126 km, the longest recorded dispersal by an African mammal
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Three African wild dog brothers have turned an already extraordinary journey into a record-breaking one, travelling 4,126 kilometres across Zambia aft.
articles.body: Three African wild dog brothers have turned an already extraordinary journey into a record-breaking one, travelling 4,126 kilometres across Zambia after leaving their pack in search of new territory. The three males departed from the Mayukuyuku Pack in Kafue National Park in July 2025 and were tracked using GPS collars as researchers followed their movements across a landscape of protected areas, game management areas, roads, reservoirs and cities. The findings, published in Ecology, document what researchers describe as the longest recorded dispersal by an African mammal. The study, led by Scott Creel of Montana State University with collaborators from the Zambian Carnivore Programme and other institutions, also provides a glimpse into the challenges faced by African wild dogs as they move between increasingly fragmented habitats.Three brothers leave their packThe three males were about three years old when they left the Mayukuyuku Pack in Kafue National Park. They were among 19 pups from the pack that had survived to adulthood. Their departure was part of a natural process known as dispersal, in which young wild dogs leave their birth group and travel in search of unrelated animals with which they can potentially form new breeding groups.The researchers were monitoring several groups of dispersing African wild dogs, making it possible to compare how different animals moved through Zambia. Four females from the same Mayukuyuku Pack had dispersed around two weeks before the males, but their movements were initially much more limited. The three brothers, by contrast, began a remarkable eastward journey that eventually took them hundreds of kilometres from their original home range.A journey through a changing landscapeThe dogs' route was not a straightforward journey between two protected areas. They moved through a mixture of protected and unprotected landscapes and encountered some major obstacles along the way. The brothers travelled towards areas around Kabwe, Kitwe and Ndola. When they approached urban areas, they changed direction rather than continuing through the cities. On one occasion, the dogs travelled north towards Ndola before turning around and retracing almost the same route for approximately 200 kilometres.Large reservoirs also forced the animals to change course. Instead of crossing the water, the brothers travelled around the reservoirs before continuing east towards the Luangwa Valley ecosystem. Their movements eventually took them towards the Chisomo and Petauke Game Management Areas, which are connected to the wider Luangwa landscape and South Luangwa National Park.4,126 kilometres on the moveThe distance travelled by the three brothers continued to increase as they moved across Zambia. By November 2025, they had already covered more than 2,300 kilometres from their original home range. The dogs later continued through the Luangwa Valley ecosystem before settling in a new range in the Luano Game Management Area, near the top of the Great Rift Escarpment.By April 1, 2026, their GPS records showed that they had travelled a total path length of 4,126 kilometres since leaving their birth pack. The 4,126-kilometre figure represents the actual route taken by the dogs rather than the straight-line distance between their start and end points. The maximum straight-line distance between the beginning and end of their journey was 419 kilometres. That distinction illustrates just how much ground the brothers covered while navigating the landscape. Instead of travelling directly towards a destination, they repeatedly changed direction to avoid obstacles and find suitable routes.Why wild dogs disperseFor African wild dogs, dispersal is closely connected to their social structure. The species lives in highly cooperative packs, and young animals eventually leave their natal groups. Dispersal allows them to search for unrelated individuals and establish new groups where breeding can occur. Long-distance movement can therefore help maintain connections between separate populations. If animals can safely move between different areas, they may encounter potential mates and contribute to genetic exchange between populations.However, the researchers point out that extremely long movements do not automatically translate into successful population connectivity. The animals may travel extraordinary distances without ultimately joining another group or producing offspring there. The three brothers' journey nevertheless demonstrates the species' remarkable mobility and the potential scale at which conservation planning must operate.Moving beyond protected areasOne of the most significant aspects of the journey was the variety of landscapes the dogs crossed. Their movements took them through national parks and game management areas as well as landscapes with much greater human influence. That creates risks for animals that depend on large territories. Roads can pose a collision risk, while livestock areas can create opportunities for conflict between predators and people. Wire snares used for bushmeat hunting can also injure or kill wild dogs.The study highlights how dispersing animals can face threats outside protected areas. This makes the spaces connecting protected landscapes important for the long-term conservation of wide-ranging species such as African wild dogs.A record that reveals a conservation challengeDiscover Wildlife, which reported on the research, described the brothers' journey as the longest recorded dispersal by an African mammal. The publication noted that the dogs' GPS-tracked movements took them across roads, around cities and reservoirs and through the dramatic terrain of Zambia's Great Rift Valley.The journey also shows that the boundaries drawn on conservation maps do not necessarily correspond to the way wildlife uses the landscape. A national park may provide a safe habitat, but a dispersing animal still needs to travel through the areas between protected sites. For African wild dogs, those connections can be particularly important because individuals may travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres when searching for new social groups and territory.Connecting Zambia's wildlife landscapesThe researchers' observations provide evidence that African wild dogs can move between some of Zambia's major wildlife areas despite the presence of human settlements and other barriers. The three brothers ultimately established themselves in the Luano Game Management Area after their extraordinary journey. Their movements demonstrate that landscapes outside national parks can also play a role in supporting wildlife movement.For conservationists, records like these can help identify routes used by animals and highlight places where maintaining habitat connectivity could matter. Protecting corridors between wildlife populations can provide dispersing animals with opportunities to move safely rather than becoming isolated in individual protected areas. The story of the three brothers is therefore about more than a remarkable distance. Their 4,126-kilometre journey shows the scale at which African wild dogs can move across their landscape and the obstacles they must navigate along the way. It also underlines a broader conservation issue: protecting wildlife may require looking beyond the boundaries of individual parks and preserving the connections that allow animals to move between them.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Stephen Hawking: "We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of…"
articles.summary: Science News: Humanity has achieved extraordinary things, from exploring distant planets to developing technologies that have transformed everyday life. Yet, despit.
articles.body: Humanity has achieved extraordinary things, from exploring distant planets to developing technologies that have transformed everyday life. Yet, despite these accomplishments, our place in the universe remains remarkably small. British physicist Stephen Hawking often encouraged people to look beyond their immediate surroundings and consider the vastness of the cosmos. His thought-provoking words, "We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the universe", offer a reflection on human origins, intelligence and curiosity. The quote invites us to think about how creatures that evolved on a small planet became capable of studying galaxies, black holes and the fundamental laws of nature.Quote of the day by Stephen Hawking"We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the universe."Stephen Hawking's quote combines humility with admiration for human intelligence. By describing humanity as an advanced breed of monkeys, he points towards our evolutionary origins and biological connection to other life forms. The reference to a minor planet orbiting an average star places Earth within the enormous scale of the cosmos. However, the second part of the quote shifts the focus from our physical limitations to our intellectual abilities. Although human beings occupy a relatively small corner of space, they possess the ability to investigate the universe and develop explanations for phenomena far beyond their immediate experience.Humanity's humble place in the universeEarth is one planet orbiting the Sun, which is a star in the Milky Way galaxy. Our galaxy contains billions of stars, while the observable universe contains an immense number of galaxies. Compared with these cosmic scales, human civilisation occupies a tiny part of space and time. Hawking's description encourages people to recognise this perspective without dismissing the importance of human life. Understanding our small physical presence can inspire curiosity about the universe and encourage people to look beyond everyday concerns. The quote therefore presents humility not as a rejection of humanity's achievements but as a way to understand them within a much larger cosmic setting.From evolutionary origins to human intelligenceThe comparison with monkeys reflects the evolutionary history of human beings. Humans belong to the primate order and share common ancestry with other primates, including modern apes. Over millions of years, evolutionary processes shaped the physical and cognitive characteristics of our species. Human intelligence eventually supported complex language, cultural development, scientific investigation and technological innovation. Hawking's wording draws attention to the contrast between our biological origins and the intellectual capabilities we have developed. The same species that evolved on Earth can use mathematics, instruments and observations to study objects located billions of light-years away.The remarkable ability to understand the cosmosThe central idea of the quote lies in the statement that humans can understand the universe. Scientific knowledge has allowed researchers to investigate the origins of stars, the behaviour of black holes and the expansion of the cosmos. Telescopes collect light from distant astronomical objects, while mathematical models help scientists explain observations and test theories. Hawking himself made significant contributions to the study of black holes, including research into the theoretical prediction that black holes can emit radiation, now known as Hawking radiation. His work illustrates how human reasoning can explore physical processes that cannot be directly experienced in everyday life.What Stephen Hawking's words teach usHawking's quote offers two connected perspectives on human existence. The first is a reminder that people should not assume that humanity occupies a central or privileged physical position in the universe. The second is an appreciation of the ability to ask questions, seek evidence and develop knowledge. These ideas remain relevant in a world where scientific discoveries continue to challenge our understanding of space and time. The quote can encourage readers to approach the unknown with curiosity while recognising the limitations of current knowledge. Its lasting appeal comes from the balance between cosmic humility and the extraordinary potential of the human mind.Why this quote remains relevant todayModern astronomy continues to reveal the complexity of the universe, from exoplanets orbiting distant stars to observations of ancient galaxies. Space missions and powerful telescopes have expanded scientific understanding, while unanswered questions continue to drive research. Hawking's words resonate with this ongoing effort because they emphasise the value of understanding rather than simply occupying a prominent place in the cosmos. Human beings may live on a small planet, but their capacity to investigate nature has opened a window into the universe. The quote ultimately encourages reflection on our origins, our achievements and the questions that remain beyond our current knowledge.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
articles.summary: The Apple Watch Series 12 adds two important hardware updates that spell out an ambitious plan for AI health and ambient sensing features.
articles.body: You wouldn’t know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables. These ideas — and this year’s updates — can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI as a way to make sense of all your health data. With the latter, Apple is potentially kicking the door down on what’s been a niche, nascent, and recently problematic market. (Either way you slice it, AI is part of the equation.) Most of the ideas explored with the Series 12 aren’t novel, but they haven’t been implemented by a company with Apple’s scale or reputation. [Product: Apple Watch Series 12 | After a week with the Series 12, I can’t say I have a complete picture. Several of the most interesting health and AI features aren’t launching until later this year and weren’t available for review. But even without them, the revamped internals provide some meaningful upgrades. So for now, this is a look at the health features that’ll be available at launch — and a preview of the wild AI ideas to come. New hardware Two key hardware updates separate the Series 12 (and the Ultra 4) from previous Apple Watches. The first is the new S11 chip, which features a secure exclave for microphone data processing on top of a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. There’s also a completely redesigned health sensor array. This new array doesn’t necessarily capture new data, but it enables the watch to measure health metrics in a more frequent, accurate, and power-efficient way. The electrodes that enable the EKG feature are larger to ensure better skin contact, the photodiodes have been reconfigured to capture reflected light more efficiently, and larger, less power-hungry optical LEDs are in place to shine light into the skin. [Image: This is a significant hardware redesign compared to previous Apple Watches. Together, these hardware upgrades enable a host of new software features, including more frequent heart rate sampling, a new readiness score, and a brave new world of Audio Intelligence, which is what Apple is calling its upcoming suite of AI-powered ambient listening features. Most notably, the redesigned sensors mean the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now capable of truly continuous heart rate monitoring. Previously, to preserve charge, Apple Watches only sampled heart rate once every five minutes when you weren’t working out. Now, the Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, both at rest and during activities. Other wearable companies have been able to do this for ages, but this is a genuinely helpful update for folks who might need to monitor heart rate due to chronic illnesses. [Image: Siri AI is more front and center in watchOS 27. Apple put out a white paper comparing how accurate its continuous heart rate monitoring is to a gold-standard Polar H10 chest strap, as well as competitors like the Pixel Watch 4, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop across several types of workouts and at rest. (It’s an interesting read for wearable nerds!) I’d need roughly eight arms and legs to replicate this study in a week, and alas, I’m not an octopus. However, I did wear an H10 chest strap during two runs (one steady state and one interval run), a walk, and while at rest. At all times, the Series 12 was within five beats per minute of the H10. There was a slight lag compared to the H10, but in regular use, you’re not going to notice that four-second difference. I’ll continue testing the Series 12 and Ultra 4 against other devices and across activity types, but I’m pretty confident the Apple Watch is now in line with many other popular wearables. The S11’s impact was also noticeable in testing. Siri AI queries are faster on the Series 12 than my Ultra 3. You still might run into latency as Siri “thinks,” but not as much. If you want more in-depth thoughts about Siri on the wrist, my opinion hasn’t changed from my watchOS 27 preview. In a nutshell, this is the most capable wrist computer Apple’s made, and adding a single pinch gesture to select items makes one-handed control the best it’s ever been. I didn’t notice a negative impact to battery life from continuous heart rate tracking. People will gripe that the Series 12 doesn’t have multi-day battery and sticks to the Series 11’s 24-hour battery estimate. But like last year, I maintain that faster charging is a fine enough solution. In a 20-minute charging test, I went from 20 to 64 percent battery. Yes, that does mean charging daily in little spurts, but I’ve yet to have the watch die on me. I vehemently believe everyone needs to let their wrists breathe daily, and showering is the perfect time to go watchless. You’ll survive 20 to 30 minutes of no data. Are you ready? All this new hardware paves the way for a much more robust health tracking experience. That’s probably why, later this fall, we’re getting a new, redesigned Health app. From the demos I’ve seen, it’s going to be a dramatic change. There’ll be AI-powered insights, a longevity tab that includes a Health Age score, VO2 max assessment tests using your phone’s camera, and even the ability to order a blood panel through Quest Diagnostics for $119. The redesigned app is currently available in the latest iOS 27 developer beta, and I’ll give my early impressions on that soon. However, in this review I’m only going to talk about what’s available to everyone at launch. The big update ready today is Apple’s take on a readiness score. Readiness scores were popularized ages ago by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop and are meant to be a digestible gauge of how well you’ve recovered from physiological stress. In essence, how “ready” you are to work out again. [Image: It takes seven days to populate the readiness score, but the Vitals app now includes extra information about your overnight vitals. Apple assesses “readiness” through a combination of overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics like activity, sleep score, and overnight vitals encompassing resting heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and a new metric called recovery heart rate variability (HRV). You might think — wait, my Apple Watch has been able to measure HRV for years. You’d be correct. This new recovery HRV metric uses a different formula and is enabled by the fact that the watch’s updated sensor array can now take any HRV measurement much more frequently. Whereas “regular” HRV is meant to be a longitudinal look at your overall stress and cardiovascular health, Apple uses recovery HRV as a gauge of your daily, short-term strain. (And because this is enabled by the new array, it does mean readiness requires at least a Series 12 or Ultra 4.) It takes a hot minute to generate the score — seven nights of sleep in which you get at least four hours of rest. On the eighth day, you wake up with a score from 0 to 10. A 0 to 1 means you should recover, a 2 to 4 means “pace yourself,” 5 to 7 is a benign “ready,” and anything 8 and above is a signal to “go for it.” My week of serious sleeping and accuracy testing culminated in a readiness score of 7. [Image: Radiant gold up top, dark bronze on the bottom. I’m of the opinion that people intuitively know whether they feel like working out or not. This is a feature that’s most useful for stubborn athletes who overtrain and need a reminder to not burn themselves out. I appreciate this isn’t a static score. A powerful nap or an extra hard workout could cause your readiness score to rise or fall during the day. For the Garmin nerds, I’d say it’s like a combination of Body Battery (which estimates your energy levels in real time) and traditional readiness scores. Given that wearable companies keep pumping out new metrics, I appreciate that Apple’s chosen to consolidate what could’ve been multiple data points into one. After WWDC, I wrote that I was relieved Apple wasn’t diving full-on into AI health coaching features. I have to eat my words a teeny bit, considering Apple is clearly starting to incorporate some — though not all — of the AI health trends I’ve seen cropping up over the past two years. So far, I think Apple is carefully weighing what trends to hop on and which ones to avoid. That’s a smart long-term move. But I’m still relieved Siri AI isn’t playing a larger part just yet. Audio Intelligence, part one Aside from faster, more power-efficient performance, the S11 chip also enables the most surprising update to the Series 12: ambient listening. That ability is what enables Audio Intelligence, a suite of four features that essentially turn the microphone into a potentially powerful AI tool. The two flashiest features are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you read a short transcript on your wrist of the past 15 seconds, while the latter is a high-level summary of conversations you’ve had during the day. In this summer of public backlash against so-called pervert glasses and Flock cameras, these two features understandably stirred up a lot of concern and emotion on social media. That said, I wasn’t able to test these features because they’re not available yet. They’ll arrive later this year via a software update. What was available to test was faster Shazam for identifying songs and sound recognition for alerting you of potentially urgent nearby noises. Both of these features require you to opt in and are not turned on by default. If you do turn on music detection, it is extremely fast. You can just pinchy pinch to bring up the Smart Stack, AI will surface the Shazam widget, and boom — there’s the song, correctly identified. (I did trip it up a teensy bit by rapidly switching between songs, but that’s not likely to happen in an organic Shazam experience.) [Image: The improved Shazam works in the Smart Stack. Here, Shazam is battling against ambient noise from a helicopter. Shazam did not win. Testing sound recognition, which is an accessibility feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, was less conclusive. It’s designed to flag on the wrist when sounds like doorbells, alarms, or sirens go off. Ironically, I haven’t had my doorbell ring this past week, but I did pull up several YouTube videos of doorbell chimes at various volumes. None triggered the feature. I think that’s a good thing. In my previous tests with other ambient listening AI wearables, they struggled to distinguish between “real” sounds and TV shows. The last thing you want is a fictional doorbell triggering an annoying, real-life alert. A blaring truck horn also didn’t trigger the feature, as it wasn’t a siren. I’ve asked Apple whether there’s specific tuning to minimize false positives, but I haven’t heard back yet. I’ll do a deeper dive into Audio Intelligence once the whole suite of features is available. But to me, it’s clear that Apple has been taking notes about the burgeoning AI wearable space. It’s a deliberate choice to introduce these features on the Apple Watch, an already familiar and beloved device. As other tech companies deal with surveillance and harassment concerns, Apple’s published a privacy white paper and support documents to position itself as a leader trying to set a new standard. If successful with the public, it’s not a stretch to see how Apple might include these kinds of features on a pair of smart glasses or, perhaps, AirPods with camera sensors. If not, it’s no big miss. The Apple Watch is already a useful, sometimes lifesaving device without Audio Intelligence. The most interesting, and perhaps consequential, piece of this rollout is that it comes from Apple, a wildly successful tech company with the strongest privacy reputation in Silicon Valley. If it can’t make this category of device work, that certainly doesn’t bode well for AI wearables as a whole. Testing the waters In many ways, this is an incomplete Series 12 review. Judging solely on what’s available today, this is a straightforward hardware upgrade that closes the gap between Apple and the standout perks of more niche rivals like Whoop and Oura. For those pondering upgrades, Apple has laid a strong foundation with its hardware for some ambitious features down the road. I’d understand if you have qualms about Audio Intelligence and privacy, and to those folks: I’ll remind you that last year’s models are still great, probably available on sale, and don’t come with as many privacy questions. [Image: I’ll be back to test everything once it’s all available, but even now you can see where Apple is heading. Otherwise, the Series 12 is a worthy upgrade if you’re sporting a Series 6 or earlier. Series 7 and 8 users should weigh how much they care about AI features versus their device’s current battery life, as watchOS 26 will continue to get security updates. Series 9 and later don’t need to upgrade unless, perhaps, they have a chronic illness that could benefit from the improved continuous heart rate monitoring. The excellent SE 3 remains my recommendation for smartwatch newbies who just want a basic fitness tracker. I’ll have an Ultra 4-specific review out soon, but I can already tell you that’s for folks who like big screens, better battery life, and aspire to the outdoor life. If the Series 12 only had a new sensor array, updated Health app, and a more useful Siri on the wrist, that’d be a significant update and win on its own. But there’s a lot more here that’s going to change this product in some fundamental ways over the next few months. I have a feeling that Apple’s ambitions for the watch don’t end with health tracking. --- Agree to Continue: Apple Watch Series 12 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. You can only use the Apple Watch Series 12 with an iPhone. That means you’ll have already agreed to the iPhone’s terms of service and privacy agreements. Optional services, like Apple Pay, Apple Music, or Fitness Plus, will also come with their own agreements. Using the Health app also comes with its own terms and conditions. Audio Intelligence features are opt-in and are not turned on by default. If you choose to enable cellular service, you’ll also have to agree to your carrier’s terms. I activated cellular on T-Mobile and was asked to agree to one mandatory agreement. If you add any third-party apps or integrations, you must also agree to those individual terms and privacy policies. Specific to the Apple Watch, you must agree to the following: * Terms and Conditions Some features, like hypertension notifications, EKG, sleep apnea, or blood oxygen monitoring, may also require you to disclose your location data, as it depends on local regulatory clearances. Final tally: One mandatory agreement plus any mandatory agreements for your iPhone. Several, several optional agreements.
